name: Felix Bauer

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, and thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal week at university so far.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm in the first year of marketing and business. I share a terraced house near the Millbank campus with three other guys. Between lectures I tutor GCSE maths for twelve pounds an hour and make social media posts for two local shops, a bike repair place and a juice bar. I use AI for nearly all of it, so one hour of tutoring prep takes ten minutes.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How did the shop work start?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The bike shop owner, Raj, was a client of my dad's old business. I offered to make his posts for fifty pounds a month. Now I've got two shops, about a hundred and twenty pounds a month, and a real portfolio. My dad doesn't have spare money, so I pay my own rent out of tutoring and the shops.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. The scenario is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a bit of a letdown but fine. The tools I already use save me time and that's enough. I'd tell friends who are waiting for something huge not to hold their breath.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be okay. My income doesn't depend on a revolution. But the money's still thin. My rent is four hundred and eighty pounds, and if Raj drops me I lose a quarter of my income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep growing the shop work. Three more clients, maybe at eighty pounds a month. I'd keep tutoring and put fifty pounds a month into a savings account. I'd also test selling a small template pack for shop owners.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine. A bit flat. Not scared.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would stay hard for you in a world where AI mostly fizzles?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Most of what I do works because the tools exist. If they stalled, I'd still have the skill of knowing what makes a post work, which isn't just the tool.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much does your side work depend on AI being useful?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay ready for clients who want something simple and cheap. That's what small shops want.

say: I'd tell friends waiting for something huge not to **hold their breath**.
I'd say the tools I use already save me enough time.
think: My income doesn't depend on a **revolution**, but rent is four hundred and eighty pounds.
If Raj drops me I lose a **quarter** of my income.
do: Sign **three more clients** at eighty pounds a month.
Keep tutoring and put fifty pounds a month into **savings**.
Test a small **template pack** for shop owners.
S0.quote: My income doesn't depend on a revolution. But the money's still thin.
fieldNote: Sees AI as a **tool**, so the plateau changes little for him.
Mood is uneasy because rent is high and one client is a quarter of income.
Entrepreneurial reflex: more clients and a product.

steps.text: Sign three more small shop clients at eighty pounds a month
Put fifty pounds a month into a savings account
Test a template pack for shop owners with my own money

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Next picture. The scenario is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's the best time ever to start something small. I'd say people who don't use the tools will be left behind. I'd post about how I use them, and offer a free workshop at the uni.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm excited and nervous. The tools are making my posts cheaper to produce, but that means the shops can do them too. In a year Raj might do his own. I need something extra beyond the posts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd move from posts to strategy: how a shop brings in customers, how to use the tools well. I'd learn a booking system and sell a monthly package. I'd keep tutoring, since I've got six regulars, and I'd put the savings into a better laptop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. It's exciting, but I can see the gap opening under my feet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which parts of your work are most at risk if AI keeps improving?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The simple post-making. If a shop owner can type a sentence and get a post, I'm not needed. Where I'm needed is knowing what to say and who to say it to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you stay ahead of the next wave?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd talk to other students running side work and share clients. A group of us could offer a full service to businesses.

say: I'd say it's the **best time ever** to start something small.
I'd offer a free **workshop** at uni on using the tools.
think: The tools make posts **cheaper**, so shops may soon do their own.
do: Move from posts to **strategy** and sell a monthly package.
Put the savings into a better **laptop**.
feel: **Uneasy**: exciting, but the gap opens under my feet.
S1.quote: If a shop owner can type a sentence and get a post, I'm not needed. Where I'm needed is knowing what to say and who to say it to.
fieldNote: Spots the **commoditising** of his own side work.
Responds by moving up to strategy, a typical adaptive move.
Plans a collective of student freelancers.
Optimism is real but sits beside a clear read of risk.

steps.text: Learn one shop booking system and sell a monthly package
Run a free workshop at uni on using AI tools
Buy a better laptop from savings
Team up with two other student freelancers to offer a full service

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Next picture. The scenario is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's historic and we should all take a breath. I'd post about practical steps people can take. I'd probably say I'm excited, because it sounds smarter to say that, even if it's partly bluster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be scared. If anyone can do what I do for free, my shops don't need me. Everything I earn is online work, and it's exactly what AI replaces. Tutoring too, if a bot can teach maths cheaper.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go for the things robots reach last. I'd spend a lot of time on people, relationships and local business. I'd save everything, cut my spending, and look at a trade or hands-on route on the side. I'd ask my uncle about his plumbing firm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'm adaptive, but this is fast even for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you protect yourself in that world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The gap is that I'd say I'm excited, then I'd lie awake. I don't think many people admit that. I'd want to be the person who acts, but the debt scares me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do about the degree?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd talk to my flatmates and pool resources. We could share costs, even rent a smaller house. It's less glamorous, but it works.

say: I'd say it's **historic** and people should take a breath.
I'd post practical **steps** people can take, and I'd try to sound excited.
think: If anyone can do what I do **for free**, the shops don't need me.
Even **tutoring** goes if a bot can teach maths cheaper.
do: Cut spending and **save** everything I can.
Ask my uncle about a **plumbing** firm apprenticeship.
Move into a smaller, **cheaper** shared house.
feel: **Anxious**, fast even for an adaptive person.
S2.quote: I'd say I'm excited, then I'd lie awake. I don't think many people admit that.
fieldNote: Notes a clear gap between **public bravado** and private fear.
Names his online income as the exposed part.
Considers a trade, which shows genuine flexibility.

steps.text: Cut spending to rent, food and travel
Save every pound from the shop and tutoring money
Ask my uncle about plumbing apprenticeships
Move to a smaller, cheaper shared house

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Next picture. The scenario is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to get ahead if you move now. I'd say learn the tools, build something, don't wait for permission. I'd write about it for other students.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd feel pretty good. By 2031 I'd be twenty-three, with a small agency of my own, if I'm lucky. The risk is that AGI makes agencies pointless. But I'd have a few years of income and savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish my degree while growing the agency, hire another student for a few hours, and keep a cash reserve of two months. I'd learn the hands-on side of business, like sales and meeting clients. I'd also try to get a placement year with a larger firm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but upbeat. I can see paths.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do differently with five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years makes me defensive. Five lets me build. By 2031 I could have a business, a bit of money, and a plan B.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you hope your income looks like by 2031?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep moving. If AGI arrives, I'd look for work in the human parts, like running events or advising shops in person.

say: I'd say five years is enough to **get ahead** if you move now.
I'd write about it for **other students**.
think: By 2031 I could have a small **agency**, savings and a few years of income.
The risk is **AGI** making agencies pointless.
do: Grow the agency while finishing the **degree**.
Apply for a **placement** year at a larger firm.
feel: **Uneasy** but upbeat, because I can see paths.
S3.quote: Two years makes me defensive. Five lets me build.
fieldNote: Time turns his stance from **defence** to building.
Plans a reserve and a placement, balancing risk.
Names a human-facing fallback in events and in-person advice.

steps.text: Hire another student for a few hours a week
Build a two-month cash reserve from client money
Apply for a placement year at a larger marketing firm
Learn sales and client meetings through short courses

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Next picture. The scenario is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty of time, and the people who win will be the ones who learn early. I'd say it's an exciting decade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be calm. By twenty-eight I could have a business, a small property or an investment. I'm adaptive. I'd rather ride the change than hide from it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the degree, run the agency, and put money into index funds. I'd also try a few other small businesses, since ten years allows failure. I'd learn new tools as they appear and keep a few human skills sharp.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. I'd feel lucky to be eighteen in this world.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With ten years, what are you building?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell a younger student to start something small now, because a decade of small experiments beats one big plan. I'd also tell them to save a bit from every pay cheque.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell younger students?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd also want to give back, maybe teach a short course for new freelancers. That's more fun than just earning.

think: By twenty-eight I could have a **business** and an investment.
I'd rather **ride** the change than hide from it.
do: Run the agency and put money into **index funds**.
Try a few other small **businesses**, since a decade allows failure.
Teach a short **course** for new freelancers.
feel: **Calm**, lucky to be eighteen in this world.
S4.quote: A decade of small experiments beats one big plan.
fieldNote: Ten years makes him **calm**, because his habits fit the change.
His plan is many small experiments rather than one bet.
Wants to teach others, a sign of confidence.

steps.text: Run the agency through the degree and add two more clients
Put forty pounds a month into an index fund
Keep three months of rent in a separate account
Try each new AI tool within a month of release

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. Everything I earn is online and could vanish at once. What would help is practical stuff, like cheap retraining, rules that stop firms dumping graduates, and some income floor for the first year.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Just that confident people are scared too. I sound upbeat, but money is thin and I carry it alone. A bit of honest talk from adults would help.

headlineQuote: Confident people are scared too. I sound upbeat, but money is thin and I carry it alone.
portrait: Felix is an eighteen-year-old **marketing** student who tutors maths and makes social posts for two local shops.
He uses AI every day, so he knows how fast his own side work could be copied.
Pragmatic and centre in politics, he moves first and builds small businesses.
His upbeat public voice hides real worry about thin savings and rent.
He's **calm** with ten years, **anxious** with two, always looking for human-facing fallbacks.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** scenario, because all his income is online work that AI could copy.
whatWouldHelp: Cheap **retraining** and an income floor for the first year.
